query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin refractory high‐entropy alloy (HEA) interlayer to the surfaces of W particles (or connected W regions) before copper infiltration will provide a metallurgically bonded, void‐free interface that suppresses phase separation and defect formation under irradiation, thereby improving thermal transport while preserving mechanical durability compared to conventional Cu infiltration methods.
generation.material_initial_state: A preformed tungsten skeleton or W particles embedded within a continuous copper matrix fabricated by conventional powder metallurgy or infiltration methods, which typically exhibit phase separation and void defects.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin (e.g., several hundred nanometers to a few micrometers) layer of a refractory HEA (such as a W–Ta–Ti–V–Cr based alloy optimized for high-temperature fusion-relevant conditions) onto the W surfaces prior to Cu infiltration; this can be implemented via vapor deposition or similar coating methods.
generation.conditions: The consolidation and subsequent service are performed under high-temperature conditions with high thermal flux and neutron/ion irradiation as expected in fusion-reactor divertor joints; processing should use compatible powder metallurgy or sintering conditions (e.g., spark plasma sintering) that preserve the fine microstructure of the HEA layer.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, well-adhered refractory HEA interlayer at the W–Cu interface that promotes diffusion bonding and minimizes void formation.
generation.mechanism: The HEA interlayer, with its inherent high mixing entropy, sluggish diffusion, and irradiation resistance, forms a stable, chemically homogeneous bond at the interface. This layer compensates for the mismatch in thermal expansion and prevents rapid phase separation and void formation during thermal cycling and irradiation; it also provides additional dispersion and solid solution strengthening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to composites prepared via direct Cu infiltration, the HEA-coated W–Cu composite is expected to exhibit reduced void content, improved thermal transport across the interface, and enhanced mechanical durability (e.g., higher yield strength and resistance to irradiation-induced embrittlement), although the precise improvement magnitude is subject to further experimental validation.
generation.baseline: A conventional W–Cu composite fabricated by infiltrating Cu into a W particle skeleton or preformed W–Cu mixture using standard powder metallurgy or infiltration techniques that often result in interfacial voids and phase separation.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is valid for high-temperature, high-flux irradiation environments as found in fusion reactor joints and is applicable when using powder metallurgy or SPS-based processing routes with subsequent irradiation exposure; it may not extend to materials processed solely by casting or other routes without interfacial control.
generation.uncertainty: The exact thickness of the HEA interlayer, its composition optimization, and the quantitative enhancement in thermal conductivity and mechanical properties under irradiation require further systematic investigation. Variability in the processing parameters (e.g., deposition technique, sintering conditions) may also influence the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of W–Cu composites: one set with the HEA interlayer applied to the W surfaces (via vapor deposition prior to Cu infiltration) and one set prepared using standard Cu infiltration without any interlayer. Both sets should be processed under identical powder metallurgy/SPS conditions and then subjected to simulated fusion-reactor conditions including high thermal flux and controlled ion irradiation.
measurements: Interfacial microstructure characterization (e.g., SEM/TEM, EDS) to assess voids and phase homogeneity
Thermal conductivity measurements across the W–Cu interface
Mechanical testing (e.g., yield strength, compressive strength) before and after irradiation
Irradiation-induced damage assessment (e.g., void formation, embrittlement indicators)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA-interlayered W–Cu composites do not show a statistically significant reduction in interfacial voids, fail to maintain improved thermal conductivity, or exhibit no superior mechanical durability (or even worse performance) under irradiation compared to the baseline samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractNuclear fusion is a promising energy source. The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor aims to study the feasibility of tokamak-type reactors and test technologies and materials for commercial use. One major challenge is developing materials for the reactor’s divertor, which supports high thermal flux. Tungsten was chosen as the plasma-facing material, while a CuCrZr alloy will be used in the cooling pipes. However, the gradient between the working temperatures of these materials requires the use of a thermal barrier interlayer between them. To this end, refractory high-entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying and sintering, and their thermal and irradiation resistance was evaluated. Both alloys showed phase growth after annealing at 1100 °C for 8 days, being more pronounced for higher temperatures (1300 °C and 1500 °C). The VFeTiTaW alloy presented greater phase growth, suggesting lower microstructural stability, however, no new phases were formed. Both (as-sintered) alloys were irradiated with Ar+ (150 keV) with a fluence of 2.4 × 1020 at/m2, as well as He+ (10 keV) and D+ (5 keV) both with a fluence of 5 × 1021 at/m2. Th

Re was also avoided in order to prevent the formation of irradiation-induced embrittling precipitates, . Titanium (Ti) and vanadium (V), representing a broader definition of refractory metals, were also selected. Ti plays a significant role in improving the sintered density,  through rapid and significant interdiffusion, mass transport through the interfaces, and rearrangements of particles, , , whereas V aids in improving the strength and hardness of refractory HEAs. Another refractory metal, chromium (Cr), was also chosen for use considering its ability to impart passivation. The low neutron activation properties of W, Ta, Ti, V and Cr also favor their selection for the development of materials for potential fusion plasma facing applications. The synthesis technique was selected considering its influence on the properties of the engineering materials; e.g., alloys undergo segregation when prepared by melting, and embrittlement and porosity are attributes of conventional sintering, whereas the low thickness of the final product is a limit of the physical vapor deposition (PVD) approach.
